So, to recap: Choose a video that resonates with you. Describe it vividly, using specific details and a compelling example. And most importantly, reflect on what you learned and how it affected you. That’s all for today’s episode. See you next time!

episodes.title: Describe an interesting conversation you had with an old person
transcript: Hello, dear listeners! Welcome to IELTS Time. I’m Archer. Today’s episode is about Speaking Part 2: Describe an interesting conversation you had with an old person. You should say who this person is, when and where you had the conversation, what you talked about, and explain why you think it was interesting. As usual, let’s listen to what Joseph has to say

Right, so, an interesting conversation with an old person… well, that would have to be with my great-aunt, Agnes. She was my grandmother’s sister, and while not ancient, she was definitely what I’d consider ‘old’ – probably in her late eighties when this conversation happened. It was a sunny afternoon, maybe two years ago, and I was visiting her at her flat. She lived in a small, cozy apartment complex specifically for seniors, so it was quiet and peaceful there.

I’d gone to help her with some things around the apartment, like changing a lightbulb and fixing a wobbly shelf. While we were having tea afterwards, she started telling me stories about her life. I’d heard bits and pieces before, of course, from family gatherings, but this time, it was different. She was really reminiscing, and I was genuinely interested.

We talked for hours. It wasn’t just polite chit-chat, you know? She told me about growing up during the war, how her family had to evacuate their city, and the hardships they faced. She talked about her first job at a textile mill, and how different things were back then. She even told me about her courtship with my great-uncle, which was quite funny. Apparently, he was incredibly shy and proposed to her through a letter!

What made the conversation so interesting, though, wasn’t just the historical details, but her perspective. She wasn’t bitter or regretful about the past. She acknowledged the difficulties, but she also focused on the good things, the resilience of people, and the simple joys in life. She talked about the importance of family and community, and how those connections had sustained her through everything. She had this incredible ability to find humour in even the most challenging situations.

I think it was interesting because it gave me a completely different view on life. I’m so caught up in my own world, my studies, my job prospects, that I often forget to appreciate the bigger picture. Talking to Great-Aunt Agnes reminded me that life is a journey, with its ups and downs, and that what truly matters are the relationships we build and the way we face adversity. It was a humbling experience, and it made me realize how much wisdom and experience older generations have to offer. I learned more than just historical facts that day; I learned about resilience, gratitude, and the importance of human connection. I’m so glad I took the time to listen to her stories, and I cherish that conversation to this day.

Joseph’s story about his great-aunt Agnes was truly moving, wasn’t it? It reminds us how valuable it is to connect with our elders. Now, to help you express yourself just as effectively, we’re going to break down some of the key vocabulary from his story. These words and phrases are especially helpful for the IELTS Speaking test, so get ready to boost your vocabulary.

First up, Joseph described his great-aunt as not ancient, but definitely old. This is a good way to acknowledge someone’s age respectfully, without using potentially offensive terms. For example, you could say, “My grandfather isn’t ancient, but he does enjoy sharing stories from his youth.” The word “ancient” is often used to describe things that are very old, like “ancient ruins,” not usually people. He mentioned she lived in an apartment complex specifically for seniors. This is a common term for a building with multiple apartments, often designed with the needs of older residents in mind. You might say, “My grandmother moved to a lovely apartment complex with a beautiful garden.” He also mentioned helping her fix a wobbly shelf. “Wobbly” is a great word to describe something that’s unstable and likely to fall. “The chair was so wobbly that I was afraid to sit on it,” is another example.

Joseph said he’d heard bits and pieces of his great-aunt’s stories before. This phrase means he’d only heard small, fragmented parts of the story, not the whole thing. You could use it like this: “I only know bits and pieces about my family history; I need to do some more research.” Then, he used the word reminiscing. This is a lovely word that means to think about pleasant things that happened in the past. It suggests a fond and thoughtful reflection. For instance, “My friends and I spent the evening reminiscing about our college days.” He also made a point of saying their conversation wasn’t just polite chit-chat. “Chit-chat” refers to light, informal conversation, often about unimportant things. You might say, “I prefer having deep conversations rather than just chit-chat.”

Joseph then recounted how his great-aunt had to evacuate her city during the war. “Evacuate” means to move people away from a dangerous place to a safer one. “The residents were ordered to evacuate the area due to the approaching hurricane,” is a good example. He also spoke about the hardships they faced. This word describes the difficult and unpleasant conditions they had to endure. For example, “Many people faced hardships during the economic recession.” He even shared the story of his great-uncle’s courtship of his great-aunt. Courtship refers to the period when two people are developing a romantic relationship, often with the intention of getting married. “The courtship between my parents lasted for two years before they got married.”

Joseph noted that his great-aunt wasn’t bitter about the past. “Bitter” describes someone who feels resentful or angry because of bad experiences. “Despite everything she’d been through, she wasn’t bitter at all,” is a good use of the word. He then used the word resilience, which is a crucial word to know. It refers to the ability to recover quickly from difficulties. For instance, “Her resilience in the face of adversity was truly inspiring.” He explained how family and community had sustained her. “Sustain” means to support or keep someone alive or going. “The love and support of her family sustained her through her illness.”

Joseph also mentioned that he often gets caught up in his own world. This phrase means to be so involved in something that you don’t pay attention to other things. “I get so caught up in my work that I sometimes forget to eat.” He learned about facing adversity. “Adversity” refers to difficult or challenging situations in life. “He learned to overcome adversity through sheer determination.” Finally, he described the experience as humbling. A humbling experience makes you realize that you are not as important or as clever as you thought you were. It often involves a sense of gratitude and perspective. “Winning the award was a humbling experience.”

So, those are some of the key vocabulary items from Joseph’s story, with example sentences to help you understand them better. Make sure you understand these words and try to use them in your own speaking practice. That brings us to the end of today’s episode. We hope you found it helpful. Thanks for listening to IELTS Time!

episodes.title: Describe a person who likes to read a lot
transcript: Hello, dear listeners! Welcome to the IELTS Time Podcast! My name is Archer. Today, we’re diving into IELTS Speaking Part 2: Describe a person who likes to read a lot. You should say: Who this person is; How you knew him or her; What he or she likes to read; And explain why you think he or she likes to read a lot. Now, let’s hear what Joseph has to say about this cue card.

Well, I have to say, when it comes to avid readers, my childhood friend Emma is the first person who pops into my mind. We grew up next door to each other, and our families were always hanging out—barbecues, holiday celebrations, you name it. Emma and I spent endless hours playing outside, but it was always obvious that she had a special thing for reading.

Even as a kid, you’d often find Emma tucked away in her favourite spot by the window, totally lost in a book. I remember how excited she got when she discovered the Harry Potter series—she couldn’t stop talking about it for days and was always urging everyone to read it too. As we got older, her taste in books grew even more diverse. She got into fantasy, mystery, and even historical fiction. Emma particularly loved novels that took her to different times and places, letting her explore experiences far beyond our little suburban bubble.
These days, she still reads a lot. I think she continues to enjoy fiction, especially stories that allow her to escape and imagine different worlds.

I think Emma’s love for reading mostly comes from her family. Both her parents are big readers, and they’ve created a home that really encourages a passion for books. They’re always sharing books and discussing stories together, making reading a family affair rather than a solo activity. This family vibe has definitely influenced Emma’s reading habits and preferences. Plus, since she’s a bit on the shy side, books give her a comfy escape to explore different worlds and perspectives without having to step out of her comfort zone.

Alright, let’s revisit Joseph’s response. He mentioned his friend Emma is an ‘avid’ reader. Now, avid doesn’t just mean she likes to read; it means she has a real ‘passion’ for it. She’s really ‘keen’ on reading, always eager to pick up a new book.
Think of it this way: She is an avid reader, always ready to explore the pages of a new book.

Remember how Joseph mentioned that Emma is the first person who ‘pops into his mind’? This means she immediately comes to his thoughts when he thinks about someone who loves to read. In other words, she is the first person who comes to mind. Think of how a favourite song pops into your mind when someone mentions your favourite band.

Joseph mentioned their families were always ‘hanging out.’ This means they spent time together socially, having fun and enjoying each other’s company. They would often have get-togethers or social gatherings.

Imagine this: A group of friends laughing together at a local park, enjoying a picnic while playing frisbee. This perfectly captures the essence of ‘hanging out’ – spending quality time together, having fun, and simply enjoying each other’s company.”

Joseph also used the phrase ‘you name it.’ This is an informal way of saying ‘and many other things.’ He was saying their families did all sorts of activities together – ‘barbecues, holiday celebrations, you name it!’ – basically everything you can imagine.” To give you an idea, they enjoyed a variety of activities together– hiking, camping, you name it!

Remember how Joseph said Emma was often ‘tucked away’ in her favourite spot? ‘Tucked away’ means she was in a cozy and secluded place, like a corner of her room or a comfy armchair. She was really ‘settled in’ and enjoying the peace and quiet while she read. For example, the child is tucked away in a cozy corner of the library, reading a captivating storybook.

Then, Joseph used the interesting phrase ‘suburban bubble.’ This refers to the sheltered environment of the suburbs. It might seem a bit ‘isolated’ from the real world. It’s like living in a small, protected world, a bit removed from the hustle and bustle of city life. But Emma, through her reading, was able to ‘escape’ that ‘bubble’ and explore different cultures and experiences. For example, growing up in the suburbs, I sometimes felt like I was living in a ‘suburban bubble’ sheltered from the realities of the wider world.

Joseph mentioned that Emma’s parents are always “sharing books and discussing stories together,” making reading a “family affair” rather than a “solo activity.” This means reading isn’t just something Emma does alone. It is a shared activity for the whole family. Everyone enjoys reading and discusses books together, making it a “group activity” rather than a “solo activity.” For example, a family affair could be a Sunday dinner where everyone contributes to cooking and enjoys the meal together. In contrast, a solo activity could be a single person going for a run in the park, enjoying being alone and focusing on their fitness.

Joseph also mentioned the ‘family vibe,’ which refers to the atmosphere created by the family. In this context, it’s a positive and supportive environment where reading is encouraged and celebrated. The family vibe is warm and welcoming toward reading. However, the term ‘family vibe’ can also be used in a negative way, depending on the context. While it generally describes the overall atmosphere of a family, this vibe can sometimes be tense, stressful, or overbearing if there is constant arguing or high expectations. For example, a family vibe could feel heavy and uncomfortable if family members are often in conflict or under significant pressure.

Finally, Joseph said books provide Emma with a ‘comfy escape.’ This means reading allows her to relax and forget about her worries. It is a ‘pleasant’ and ‘stress-free’ way for her to explore different worlds and perspectives. ‘Comfy’ is short for comfortable, and ‘escape’ implies a temporary departure from reality, a break from the stresses and anxieties of daily life. For example, finding a comfy spot with a good book can provide a pleasant escape from the day’s worries.

So there you have it! We’ve explored some key vocabulary from Joseph’s response. We learned that ‘avid’ describes someone with a real passion for something, like Emma’s love for reading. We also learned that ‘pop into one’s mind’ means something comes to mind instantly, like when you think of your best friend.

We discussed phrases like ‘hanging out’ to describe spending time socially, ‘you name it’ for including many things, and ‘tucked away’ for being in a cozy spot. We even explored the concept of a ‘suburban bubble,’ which refers to the sheltered life of the suburbs.

We also learned about the difference between a ‘family affair’ and a ‘solo activity,’ and how a ‘family vibe’ can encourage certain activities. Finally, we discovered how reading can provide a ‘comfy escape’ from daily stresses.
That wraps up today’s episode! Thanks for listening. Take care and see you next time!

Speaker: Finn
What did you like to do with paper as a child?

I used to draw a lot, actually. I’d spend hours sketching superheroes, cars, and all sorts of random things. I also remember making paper aeroplanes and seeing whose paper aeroplane could fly the furthest. Nothing particularly creative, but I really enjoyed it.
Have you made any crafts with paper?

Yeah, quite a few, actually, especially when I was at school. I remember making origami animals and paper decorations for art projects. I’m not particularly good at it, though. I tend to get a bit impatient when something requires too much folding or precision.
How often do you use paper in your daily life?

Not as much as I used to, to be honest. I do occasionally use it to jot down shopping lists or make quick notes, but most of my daily tasks are done digitally. I suppose my smartphone has replaced paper in quite a few aspects of my life.
Do you carry paper and pens with you when you go out?

Not really. I used to carry a small notebook around, but these days I just use my phone to take notes or set reminders. That said, I always have a pen in my backpack because you never know when you might need one, especially when filling out forms.
Do you prefer writing on paper or typing on a computer? Why?

I’d say typing, especially when I’m writing something lengthy. It’s much quicker, and I can easily edit or rearrange things without having to rewrite the whole page. Having said that, I still prefer handwriting when I’m brainstorming ideas because I find it helps me think more clearly.
Do you still write physical letters?

Very rarely, if at all. I mean, pretty much everyone I know uses messaging apps these days, so there’s not much need to write letters by hand. Having said that, I’d quite like to write one to a close friend or family member someday. It feels a bit more personal than sending a text.
Do people still keep handwritten letters today?

To be honest, I’m not really sure. I don’t know anyone who actually keeps handwritten letters, at least not among my friends or family. Most people I’m close to communicate through text messages or social media, so I can’t really imagine them holding on to physical letters. I suppose some older people might still do that, but it’s not something I’ve come across personally.
Do you think people use paper less frequently nowadays than they did in the past?

Yeah, I’d say so. I mean, just thinking about my own life, I hardly use paper at all these days. I do almost everything on my phone or laptop, whether it’s taking notes, reading the news or keeping track of appointments. Even when I need to make a shopping list, I just put it on my phone. So, I imagine quite a lot of people are in the same boat.
Do you think paper will disappear completely in the future? Why or why not?

I don’t think so, personally. I mean, I can’t see myself giving up physical books or notebooks completely. There’s just something quite satisfying about flicking through the pages of a real book, and I find it easier to concentrate when I’m reading on paper rather than on a screen. So, even if I end up using less paper in the future, I think I’ll always have some use for it.
Speaker: Blondie
What did you like to do with paper as a child?

Oh, as a kid, I was totally obsessed with origami! My grandma taught me how to fold those classic paper cranes and little jumping frogs, and I’d spend hours surrounded by colorful square sheets. Beyond that, like most children, I did a ton of doodling and made homemade birthday cards for my friends and family—usually covered in far too much glitter and stick-figure drawings.
Have you made any crafts with paper?

Yeah, definitely! Apart from all the origami I did growing up, I actually got really into scrapbooking during high school. I used to collect Polaroids and ticket stubs, as well as magazine clippings, and put them together to create collage pages. More recently, I tried my hand at making paper flowers to decorate a friend’s birthday party. It took forever and tested my patience, but the end result was surprisingly pretty!
How often do you use paper in your daily life?

To be honest, not as often as I used to, but it still pops up daily. I keep a physical notepad on my desk for quick notes or my daily to-do list because I find ticking things off on paper super satisfying. But for major tasks like writing essays or planning, I rely almost entirely on my laptop or phone.
Do you carry paper and pens with you when you go out?

Rarely, if I’m being completely honest. Unless I know I’m going somewhere where I’ll need to fill out physical forms, I just rely on my phone. My Notes app is much more convenient when I’m out, and if I ever need to jot down a quick thought or a shopping list, I just use my phone.
Do you prefer writing on paper or typing on a computer? Why?

It really depends on what I’m doing. If I’m writing a long report or an email, typing on a laptop is a no-brainer because it’s so much faster, and I can edit on the fly. That said, if I’m brainstorming or journaling, I actually prefer pen and paper—there’s something about the tactile feeling of writing by hand that helps me think more creatively.
Do you still write physical letters?

Hardly ever nowadays. Communication is so instant these days, thanks to text messages, social media and emails. However, I do make an exception for special occasions like birthdays or holidays. I’ll write a handwritten card or a short note to close friends and family because it feels much more personal and thoughtful than just sending a quick text.
Do people still keep handwritten letters today?

I can’t speak for everyone, but I know I definitely do! I’ve actually got a little memory box in my wardrobe where I keep birthday cards, postcards and handwritten notes from friends. Every now and then, I’ll look through them, and it’s lovely because they bring back so many memories. I don’t think old text messages have quite the same sentimental value.
Do you think people use paper less frequently nowadays than they did in the past?

In my case, definitely. When I was at school, I used to carry around a planner, a diary and several notebooks, so I went through quite a lot of paper. These days, though, I do almost everything on my iPad or laptop, including taking notes and organising my schedule. I honestly can’t remember the last time I bought a notebook!
Do you think paper will disappear completely in the future? Why or why not?

I doubt it, actually. I mean, even though I do most things digitally, I still love buying physical copies of my favourite novels. I’ve got quite a few on my bookshelf, and I just enjoy holding a real book and turning the pages. I also think handwritten cards will always have a place, especially for birthdays and special occasions. So, I reckon we’ll use less paper in the future, but I can’t see it disappearing completely.

episodes.title: Losing Things
transcript: Loading video…
Speaker: Finn
Do you often lose things?

Not particularly, although I do have my moments. I’m generally quite organised, but I sometimes misplace things like my keys or my phone, especially when I’m in a rush. Thankfully, I usually find them after a bit of searching.
What kinds of things do you usually lose?

Probably small everyday items, like my keys, earphones and wallet. They’re easy to misplace because I tend to put them down without really thinking. I’ve actually got into the habit of checking my pockets before leaving the house.
When was the last time you lost something important?

I think it was a couple of months ago when I misplaced my wallet. I was pretty stressed because it had my bank cards and driving licence in it. Luckily, I found it underneath the passenger seat of my car, so it wasn’t quite the disaster I’d imagined.
How do you usually feel when you lose something?

I get quite frustrated, to be honest, particularly if it’s something I use every day. I usually start retracing my steps and trying to remember where I last had it. If I can’t find it after a while, I get a little anxious, especially if it’s valuable.
What do you usually do when you can’t find something?

The first thing I do is check the obvious places, like my desk, my pockets or the sofa. If it’s still nowhere to be found, I try to retrace my steps and think about where I last used it. I find that staying calm is important because panicking doesn’t really help.
Do you prefer to look for lost things immediately or wait until later?

I’d rather look for them straight away, especially if they’re important. Otherwise, I know I’ll keep thinking about it and won’t be able to concentrate on anything else. That said, if I’m in a hurry, I’ll sometimes leave it until I have more time to search properly.
Have you ever found something that someone else had lost?

Yes, actually. I once found a mobile phone on a bench in a shopping centre. I handed it in to the customer service desk rather than keeping it, as I thought the owner would probably come looking for it. Hopefully, they managed to get it back.
What would you do if you found someone’s lost belongings?

I’d try to return them to their owner, if possible. If I found something like a wallet or a phone, I’d hand it in to the nearest reception desk or lost property office. I think it’s just common courtesy, and I’d hope someone would do the same for me.
Do you think people are more likely to lose things nowadays? Why?

Possibly, yes. I think people are more distracted than they used to be, mainly because we’re constantly checking our phones or thinking about several things at once. We’re also carrying more gadgets and personal belongings around, so there’s simply more stuff we can misplace.
Speaker: Blondie
Do you often lose things?

Not nearly as much as I used to, thankfully! I think I’ve become a bit more organised as I’ve got older, but I’d be lying if I said I never misplace anything. It still happens every now and then, usually when I’m rushing or stressed out, but it’s much rarer these days.
What kinds of things do you usually lose?

Oh, it’s almost always the small, everyday essentials—things like my house keys, my transit card, or occasionally lip balm. They tend to disappear into the bottom of my bag or get left in random places around the apartment, like the kitchen counter or between the sofa cushions.
When was the last time you lost something important?

Actually, it was just a couple of weeks ago. I misplaced my ID holder while I was running errands, and I started to panic because it had several important cards in it. Thankfully, I retraced my steps and realised I’d left it sitting on a café table. I was so relieved when I got it back!
How do you usually feel when you lose something?

Initially, I get this sinking feeling in my stomach, especially if it’s something valuable or difficult to replace. It’s super frustrating, and I tend to get a bit annoyed with myself for being careless. But once the panic settles down, I usually try to switch into problem-solving mode rather than just stressing out.
What do you usually do when you can’t find something?

Well, I usually start by retracing my steps mentally—trying to remember the last time I had it in my hand. Then I systematically check all the usual places, like my desk, my coat pockets, or my bag. If it’s my phone that’s missing, I’ll borrow someone else’s phone to call mine and listen for the ringtone!
Do you prefer to look for lost things immediately or wait until later?

Oh, definitely immediately! I can’t relax at all if I know something is missing; it completely distracts me. Even if it’s late at night, I’d rather spend twenty minutes searching my room than lie in bed wondering where it is.
Have you ever found something that someone else had lost?

Yes, actually! A few months ago, while I was walking through a park, I spotted a student ID card lying right on the pavement. I knew how stressful losing something like that could be, so I handed it in to the nearby campus security office straight away.
What would you do if you found someone’s lost belongings?

If it were something like a phone or an ID card with contact details, I’d try to reach out to the owner directly or hand it in to a nearby police station or lost-and-found office. If it was something small, like a set of keys, I’d probably give it to a nearby staff member so the owner could collect it later.
Do you think people are more likely to lose things nowadays? Why?

In some ways, yes, absolutely. People lead such fast-paced, multitasking lifestyles nowadays, constantly juggling phones, laptops, and endless errands, which makes us much more easily distracted. On the flip side, though, we do have useful technology now, like Bluetooth trackers and GPS tags, that makes finding lost items a lot easier than it used to be!

Speaker: Finn
Do you often feel tired?

Not really, to be honest. I’ve usually got quite a lot of energy, and I enjoy keeping myself busy, whether that’s going out with friends or exploring the city. Unless I’ve stayed up really late the night before, I don’t tend to feel tired during the day.
What usually makes you feel tired?

Probably not getting enough sleep, to be honest. If I stay up late watching videos or playing video games with my friends, I can feel a bit sleepy the next morning. Other than that, I don’t get tired very easily, even when I’ve got quite a few things to do.
What do you usually do when you feel tired?

It depends, really. If I’m at home, I might lie down for a bit or watch something on my phone. If I’m out with friends, though, I usually just carry on with whatever we’re doing. I don’t normally need a long rest unless I’m really short on sleep.
Do you think you get enough sleep?

Yeah, most of the time. I try to get around seven or eight hours a night, although I sometimes stay up later than I should, especially if I’m watching something interesting or playing video games with my friends. I can usually manage the next day, but I definitely feel better when I’ve had a good night’s sleep.
Do you feel tired after doing exercise or other physical activities?

Not usually, unless I’ve been doing something pretty intense for a long time. I enjoy things like playing football with my friends or walking around the city, and I usually have plenty of energy to keep going. If anything, I feel better after doing something active than after sitting at home all day.
Have you ever felt exhausted after a particularly busy day?

Not really, at least not to the point of being completely exhausted. Even if I’ve spent most of the day out with friends or doing different activities, I usually still have enough energy to relax or play video games when I get home. I’d probably only feel completely drained if I’d had several late nights in a row.
What do you do to regain your energy when you feel tired?

Honestly, I don’t usually have to do much. I’ll grab something to eat, get some fresh air, or just take a short break. Sometimes, if I’ve been sitting around for too long, going outside and doing something actually makes me feel more awake.
Do you think you get tired more easily now than you did a few years ago?

Not really. I haven’t noticed much difference in my energy levels. I suppose I’ve got a few more responsibilities now than I did when I was younger, but I still enjoy going out and keeping busy. As long as I’m getting enough sleep, I can usually get through a full day without feeling particularly tired.
Speaker: Blondie
Do you often feel tired?

Yeah, fairly often, actually. Working full-time takes up quite a bit of my energy, and by the time I get home and sort out a few things, I’m sometimes ready to just sit down and do nothing. It’s not every day, though, and I usually feel fine after a good night’s sleep.
What usually makes you feel tired?

Mostly work, I think. I’m on my laptop for hours every day, so by the end of the afternoon, my eyes feel strained, and my brain’s pretty much fried. And if I haven’t slept well the night before, I definitely find it harder to concentrate.
What do you usually do when you feel tired?

I usually get up from my desk and stretch a bit, or make myself a cup of coffee. If I’ve been staring at my screen for hours, I find it helps to step away for a few minutes. And if I’m really tired at home, I’ll sometimes have a quick nap.
Do you think you get enough sleep?

Probably not, to be honest. I aim for seven or eight hours, but I often end up staying up late scrolling through my phone or reading. I can usually manage the next day, but I definitely feel better when I go to bed earlier.
Do you feel tired after doing exercise or other physical activities?

Yeah, sometimes, especially if I’ve been walking around all day or doing something physically demanding. But I actually enjoy that kind of tiredness because I feel like I’ve done something worthwhile. It’s quite different from feeling drained after sitting at my desk all day.
Have you ever felt exhausted after a particularly busy day?

Oh, definitely. Last month, we were finishing a big project at work just as I was moving into a new apartment. By the end of the week, I was completely wiped out. I ended up spending most of Sunday on the couch because I just didn’t have the energy to do anything.
What do you do to regain your energy when you feel tired?

I usually go for a short walk or get some fresh air, especially if I’ve been sitting at my desk all day. I might also grab something to eat or make a cup of tea. Sometimes, just getting away from work for ten minutes is enough to help me feel more awake.
Do you think you get tired more easily now than you did a few years ago?

Definitely, I think so. When I was a student, my schedule was more flexible, and I could stay up late without worrying too much about the next day. Now that I’m working full-time, I have to be a bit more careful with my time. If I don’t get enough sleep, I notice it much more than I used to.

episodes.title: Fruit and Vegetables
transcript: Loading video…
Speaker: Finn
How often do you eat fruit and vegetables?

I eat fruit pretty regularly, probably a few times a week, mainly because it’s convenient to grab an apple or a banana between classes. Vegetables, on the other hand, are a different story. Since I live in a dorm without a kitchen, I don’t really cook, so I tend to eat whatever’s available on campus. I’m not someone who goes out of their way to eat healthily, to be honest. Taste and convenience matter more to me.
What are your favourite fruits and vegetables?

I’m quite fond of mangoes and strawberries because I have a bit of a sweet tooth, and I really enjoy their sweet, juicy flavour. As for vegetables, I wouldn’t say I have a particular favourite, to be honest. I’m a bit picky when it comes to vegetables, and I tend to prefer foods that are more flavourful. That said, I’m happy to eat most vegetables if they’re cooked well.
Where do you usually buy fruit and vegetables?

I usually buy fruit and other essentials from the supermarket near my university. I go there pretty regularly to pick up things like bananas, apples, snacks and toiletries, so it’s convenient to get everything in one trip. I rarely buy vegetables, though, mainly because I don’t really cook for myself. I tend to buy things that are easy to eat or require little preparation.
What kind of fruits and vegetables do you dislike?

I’m not a huge fan of grapefruit because it’s quite bitter, and I’d much rather eat something sweet, like a mango or a peach. When it comes to vegetables, I’m not particularly keen on bitter greens or Brussels sprouts. I suppose I’m a bit picky when it comes to food. I’m more likely to eat vegetables if they’re well-seasoned or served with something tasty, rather than just boiled and served on their own.
Were there any fruits or vegetables you didn’t like when you were a child?

Yeah, definitely. I used to hate broccoli and spinach when I was a kid, mainly because I found their texture and flavour quite unpleasant. My parents would encourage me to eat them, but I wasn’t having any of it. I was much more interested in things like chips and sweets. I’m a little less fussy now, but I still wouldn’t choose vegetables over a good burger or a pizza. Taste has always been a big thing for me.
Do you prefer eating fresh fruit or drinking fruit juice?

I’d probably choose fresh fruit, although I enjoy a glass of orange juice now and then. Fresh fruit feels a bit more satisfying, and I like being able to eat it straight away without having to prepare anything. That’s especially convenient when I’m rushing between lectures. Having said that, if I’m buying a drink from a supermarket, I’d sometimes go for fruit juice simply because it’s refreshing and tastes good.
Is it easy to find fresh fruit and vegetables where you live?

Yeah, definitely. There’s a supermarket quite close to my dorm, so getting fresh fruit is never really a problem. They sell everything from bananas and apples to seasonal fruits, and the prices are generally reasonable. Vegetables are easy to find as well, of course, but I don’t buy them. Since I can’t cook in my dorm, I usually just get my meals from the university canteen or nearby restaurants.
Do people in your country like planting vegetables?

I’d say some people do, particularly older people or those who have gardens and enjoy spending time outdoors. Growing your own vegetables can be quite rewarding, since you get to see them grow and eventually use them in your meals. However, I don’t think it’s especially common among university students. Most of us live in dorms or small flats, and we’re usually too busy with classes and assignments to take up gardening as a hobby.
Did you grow any fruits or vegetables at home when you were a child?

No, not really. My family didn’t have a vegetable garden, and none of us was particularly interested in gardening. We just bought our fruit and vegetables from the supermarket like most people do. I remember occasionally helping my parents with small household tasks, but growing food wasn’t something we ever did. To be honest, I was much more interested in eating the food than finding out where it came from!
Speaker: Blondie
How often do you eat fruit and vegetables?

I eat them pretty much every single day, to be honest. I usually have fruit with breakfast, like berries in my oatmeal, and I make a conscious effort to include at least one or two servings of vegetables with both lunch and dinner. It’s just become an ingrained habit at this point, and I honestly feel a bit sluggish if I go a day without enough greens.
What are your favourite fruits and vegetables?

Honestly, I’m a huge fan of berries, especially raspberries and blueberries. I love their sweet yet slightly tart flavour, and I find them really refreshing. As for vegetables, I’d have to go with sweet potatoes and spinach. Spinach is super versatile, and roasted sweet potatoes have that rich, naturally sweet flavour and soft texture that’s hard to beat.
Where do you usually buy fruit and vegetables?

Most of the time, I just grab them from the local supermarket near my apartment during my weekly grocery run because it’s convenient. But on weekends, if I have time, I prefer heading to a nearby farmers’ market. The produce there tends to be fresher, often locally grown, and I find it tastes a lot better than what you get on supermarket shelves.
What kind of fruits and vegetables do you dislike?

I’ve never really been able to stand papaya—the smell and the mushy texture just don’t sit well with me. When it comes to veggies, raw celery is definitely at the bottom of my list. I find the stringy texture pretty off-putting, though I don’t mind it as much if it’s cooked down in a soup or broth.
Were there any fruits or vegetables you didn’t like when you were a child?

Oh, definitely! I absolutely hated broccoli when I was a kid. My parents always tried to get me to eat it, but I just found it super bitter. Strangely enough, as I got older and started roasting it with a bit of olive oil and garlic, my taste buds completely changed. Now it’s actually one of my go-to side dishes.
Do you prefer eating fresh fruit or drinking fruit juice?

I’d definitely opt for whole, fresh fruit. Juice can be refreshing, but I find eating whole fruit more satisfying, and I like the texture as well. Plus, some fruit juices contain quite a bit of added sugar, so I generally prefer getting my fruit in its natural form.
Is it easy to find fresh fruit and vegetables where you live?

Extremely easy, yeah. I live in a fairly urban area, so there are several grocery stores and neighbourhood greengrocers within walking distance of my place. They’re usually well-stocked with a great variety of seasonal produce, so getting fresh ingredients is never an issue.
Do people in your country like planting vegetables?

It really depends on where you live. Older generations and people living in suburban or rural areas often enjoy gardening and keep small vegetable patches in their backyards. However, among young adults or people living in city apartments, it’s less common due to space constraints, though some people still grow herbs and vegetables on their balconies.
Did you grow any fruits or vegetables at home when you were a child?

We did! My family had a small garden patch in our backyard, and we used to grow cherry tomatoes, mint, and some strawberries. I remember being super excited as a kid, checking on the tomatoes every day to see if they’d turned red yet. It was a fun little project, and tasting something you grew yourself is always really rewarding.

At home, though, I usually listen to music through my speakers, so I don’t have much reason to wear headphones unless I want some privacy.
What kind of headphones do you usually use?

I have a pair of wireless over-ear headphones. I like them because they’re comfortable to wear for a couple of hours, and the sound quality is pretty good. They’re a little bulky to carry around, though, so I mainly use them at home or when I’m studying somewhere quiet.
When do you usually wear headphones?

Mostly when I’m studying or listening to music on my own. For example, if I’m working on an assignment in the library, I’ll put them on to drown out conversations and other distractions. I don’t usually wear them when I’m walking around campus because I’d rather be aware of what’s going on around me.
Do you prefer using wired or wireless headphones? Why?

I’d definitely go for wireless headphones. I just find them more convenient because I don’t have to deal with cables getting tangled up or caught on things. The only downside is that I have to charge them every now and then, but that’s not a big deal. Overall, I think the freedom of movement makes them worth it.
How much money would you be willing to spend on a pair of headphones?

Probably around a hundred dollars, give or take. Since I’m still a university student, I can’t really justify spending hundreds of dollars on headphones, even if they’re made by a premium brand. I’d rather find something that’s comfortable, sounds good, and lasts a few years. I think there’s a point where paying more doesn’t necessarily mean you’re getting much better value.
Have you ever bought headphones online?

Yeah, I bought my current pair online a while ago. It was pretty straightforward because I could compare different models, read customer reviews, and find one that fit my budget. The only thing I couldn’t do was try them on before buying them, so I had to rely on other people’s opinions about how comfortable they were.
Do you think headphones are important in your daily life?

I’d say they’re useful, but I wouldn’t call them essential. I mainly use them when I need to focus or want to enjoy music without disturbing other people. That said, I can easily get through the day without them. I suppose they’re more of a convenience than something I absolutely can’t live without.
Do you prefer listening to music through headphones or through speakers? Why?

I’d probably choose speakers most of the time, especially when I’m at home. I like being able to move around freely without having anything on my head, and the sound feels more natural to me. However, headphones are better when I want to concentrate on the music or avoid disturbing my roommates. So, I guess it depends on where I am and what I’m doing.
Speaker: Blondie
Do you often use headphones?

Oh, constantly! I’d say I use them every single workday. Between jumping on back-to-back virtual meetings, listening to podcasts during my commute, and tuning out office chatter when I really need to concentrate on a project, they’re pretty much an essential part of my daily routine.
What kind of headphones do you usually use?

I use a pair of wireless over-ear noise-canceling headphones for working at my desk, and smaller in-ear wireless earbuds when I’m traveling or running errands. The noise cancellation is a lifesaver when I’m trying to focus or hear people clearly during calls.
When do you usually wear headphones?

Mainly during my morning and evening commute on the train, and throughout the workday when I’m concentrating on a task. I also pop them on whenever I go for a run after work to unwind and switch off from work mode.
Do you prefer using wired or wireless headphones? Why?

Wireless, without a doubt. When you’re using a laptop, a phone, and moving around your workspace, dealing with tangled cords is just a headache. The freedom of movement you get with Bluetooth headphones makes them much more practical for a busy routine.
How much money would you be willing to spend on a pair of headphones?

Since I rely on them so heavily for both work and personal use, I’d be comfortable spending around $200 to $300. I look at it as a worthwhile investment in comfort and productivity, as long as the battery life and sound quality are solid.
Have you ever bought headphones online?

Yeah, almost all my tech gear I buy online. It’s just so much more convenient to compare specs, read professional reviews, and check user feedback before making a choice. Plus, you can usually snag a good deal during seasonal sales.
Do you think headphones are important in your daily life?

Definitely. They’re essential for my job, given how many video calls I handle daily. But beyond work, they give me a sense of personal space and a way to unwind after a long day when I just want to immerse myself in music or an audiobook.
Do you prefer listening to music through headphones or through speakers? Why?

It really depends on what I’m doing. During the day, headphones are my go-to for concentration and clarity. But over the weekend, when I’m cooking dinner or relaxing at home, I much prefer playing music through a wireless speaker to fill the apartment with sound.

episodes.title: Rubbish and Recycling
transcript: Loading video…
Speaker: Finn
Is waste sorting common in your country?

Well, it’s quite common, especially in big cities, at least in theory. There are different bins for different types of waste, and people are supposed to sort everything before throwing it away. But honestly, I don’t think most people actually bother. A lot of people just put everything in one bag and take it downstairs to one of the large communal bins.
What kind of rubbish do you usually have at home?

Mostly food waste and packaging, I’d say. There’s quite a lot of plastic, things like wrappers, containers and bottles, as well as cardboard from deliveries. I don’t really separate it as I go, though. I normally just put everything in the same rubbish bag.
How do you recycle things like paper and plastic?

To be honest, I don’t really recycle them separately. I know we’re supposed to, and there are separate bins for paper and plastic, but at home I usually just put everything in the same bag. When I take it downstairs, I just put the bag into one of the large communal bins.
Do you usually separate your rubbish before throwing it away?

Not really, no. I know that’s what you’re supposed to do, but most people I know don’t bother doing it at home. It’s much easier just to put everything in one bag and take it outside. I guess if there were a stricter system, people might be more likely to sort it properly.
What do you usually do with empty bottles and cans?

If I’m at home, they normally just go into the same rubbish bag as everything else. Sometimes I’ll keep a few bottles if there’s a recycling collection or a separate bin nearby, but I wouldn’t say I do it consistently. Most of the time, I just throw them away with the rest of my rubbish.
Did you recycle when you were a kid?

Not really, no. I knew that recycling existed, but my family didn’t have a strict system at home. We’d basically put our household rubbish into a bag and take it outside. I think I became more aware of recycling later on, when I started living in a big city.
What do you do when you see rubbish on the street?

Honestly, I usually just walk past it. Unless I’ve dropped it myself, I don’t normally pick up other people’s rubbish. Even if there’s a bin nearby, I probably wouldn’t bother. I know it’s not particularly responsible, but I think that’s fairly normal where I live.
Are there many recycling bins in the place where you live?

Yeah, there are quite a few. You’ll usually find separate bins for things like plastic, paper, and general waste, especially in residential areas. The funny thing is, though, that people don’t always use them properly. It’s pretty common to see different types of rubbish mixed together in the same bin.
Do you think people in your country produce too much rubbish?

Yeah, definitely. I think we throw away a lot of packaging and disposable stuff, and online shopping has probably made it worse. But at the same time, I don’t think most people are deliberately wasteful. It’s just convenient to buy things, use them and throw the packaging away.
What do you do to reduce the amount of rubbish you produce?

Honestly, not a huge amount. I try not to waste food, and sometimes I’ll reuse a shopping bag rather than getting a new one. But apart from that, I probably produce a fairly normal amount of rubbish. I know there are things I could do differently, but it’s not something I actively think about every day.
Speaker: Blondie
Is waste sorting common in your country?

Oh, absolutely. Especially in cities, the rules can be surprisingly strict. Every area has its own system for separating things like burnable waste, non-burnable waste, plastics, and cans. But if I’m being completely honest, when you’re a busy adult working late, trying to remember which category a particular plastic container belongs in can feel like a psychological test.
What kind of rubbish do you usually have at home?

Mostly food packaging, takeaway containers, and plastic bottles. Since I work long hours, I end up buying quite a lot of ready-made meals or getting takeaway. Even when you buy something pretty simple, there’s often a surprising amount of packaging, so the plastic pile grows pretty quickly.
How do you recycle things like paper and plastic?

I try my best, but honestly, it’s a chore. For plastic bottles, you’re technically supposed to rinse them, peel off the label, and separate the cap. If I have time on the weekend, I’ll do it properly. But on a Tuesday night when I’m exhausted? Sometimes I just shove it into whatever bin is closest and hope for the best.
Do you usually separate your rubbish before throwing it away?

I have to, really. Otherwise, they can leave my rubbish bag behind with a warning sticker. It happened to me once when I accidentally put a plastic tray in the burnable bag, and it was so embarrassing. So now I sort it out of pure fear of social shame, not necessarily because I love doing it.
What do you usually do with empty bottles and cans?

If I’m out, I usually look for a recycling bin, though some of them are specifically for bottles and cans. At home, I rinse them out and save them for the collection day. My building has a particular day for bottles and cans, so I normally just keep them until then.
Did you recycle when you were a kid?

Not really by choice, but my parents were pretty strict about it. My mom used to wash out bottles and flatten milk cartons religiously. Back then it just felt like an annoying household rule, but it definitely drilled the habit into me, so sorting trash now is just second nature.
What do you do when you see rubbish on the street?

Honestly? I usually just walk past it. If it’s something I’ve dropped myself, obviously I’ll pick it up, but I wouldn’t normally pick up someone else’s rubbish. And since there aren’t always bins around, I’d have to carry it with me, so I’d probably just leave it.
Are there many recycling bins in the place where you live?

Not really on the streets. You can sometimes walk for quite a while without seeing a public trash can. But at my apartment building, we have a designated, enclosed garbage collection area on the ground floor where everyone sorts their bags into the building’s large bins.
Do you think people in your country produce too much rubbish?

Oh, 100%. People tend to use a lot of disposable packaging, and if you look at what gets thrown away every day, there’s a huge amount of plastic. It’s convenient, obviously, but sometimes you buy one small thing and somehow end up with three layers of packaging around it.
What do you do to reduce the amount of rubbish you produce?

I carry a reusable shopping bag in my backpack so I don’t have to use plastic bags when I’m shopping, and I use a reusable water bottle. But aside from those basic habits, my daily routine still generates way more packaging waste than I’d like to admit.

Speaker: Finn
Do you live in a house or a flat?

I live in a house with my parents. It’s a pretty typical family home, I’d say—not huge, but definitely big enough for the three of us. It’s in a fairly quiet neighborhood, which I really like, and there are a few shops and cafés just around the corner.
Which is your favorite room?

Definitely my bedroom. I mean, it’s probably the one place in the house where I can shut the door and have some privacy. I’ve got my computer, a decent speaker setup, and pretty much everything I need in there, so I tend to spend a lot of my free time in it.
Can you describe it?

Yeah, sure. It’s a fairly simple room, but it’s quite cozy. There’s a bed against one wall, a desk by the window, and a wardrobe that takes up far too much space. I’ve also got a few posters and some photos on the walls. It’s not exactly Instagram-worthy, but it feels like my space, which is what matters.
How long have you lived there?

Pretty much all my life, actually. My parents moved there when I was very young, so I don’t really remember living anywhere else. I suppose that’s why I’m quite attached to the place. There are loads of little memories there, even things like having friends over when I was a kid.
What do you like most about it?

Probably how comfortable it is. It’s not the kind of house that looks particularly impressive from the outside, but once you’re inside, it feels really homely. And I like having a bit of outdoor space as well. In the warmer months, I sometimes sit in the garden in the evening and just listen to music.
Can you describe the view from your windows?

From my bedroom window, I can see our back garden and a few of the houses further down the street. There are quite a lot of trees around, so it’s actually quite nice, especially in the morning. It’s obviously not some amazing city skyline, but I’d take trees and greenery over a wall of concrete any day.
If you could improve one thing about your home, what would it be?

Hmm, probably the kitchen. It’s a little cramped, especially when more than one person is trying to use it at the same time. I’d love to have a bit more counter space. My mum would probably agree with that, actually.
Do you plan to live there in the future?

I’m not really sure, to be honest. I’m happy living there at the moment, and there’s no particular reason for me to move out right now. But at some point, I’d like to have my own place and experience what it’s like to live independently. I just don’t feel the need to rush into it.
Speaker: Blondie
Do you live in a house or a flat?

I currently live in a rented flat on the third floor of a fairly modern building. It’s quite compact, but it really suits my lifestyle at the moment since it’s just me and my cat. I also like that everything I need is pretty close by.
Which is your favorite room?

Honestly, I’d have to say the living area. The whole flat is open-plan, so the living room basically flows into the kitchen, but I’ve created a little corner by the window with my sofa and a few plants. It’s probably the coziest spot in the whole flat, so I tend to spend quite a lot of time there.
Can you describe it?

Sure. I’ve got a comfortable L-shaped sofa by the window, a couple of bookshelves, and probably more houseplants than I actually need. There’s also a little side table where I usually keep my coffee or a book. I’ve painted one of the walls a soft sage green, which I really like. It’s not particularly fancy, but it feels very much like my own space.
How long have you lived there?

I’ve been living there for just over two years now. I moved in shortly after finishing my degree, and it actually felt like home pretty quickly. I think having my own place for the first time made a big difference. I really enjoyed being able to decorate it exactly how I wanted.
What do you like most about it?

Probably the location. It’s on a fairly quiet residential street, so it’s peaceful, but there are loads of cafés and little shops just a few minutes away. There’s this café I really like where I often grab a matcha in the morning, so that’s become part of my routine.
Can you describe the view from your windows?

The main window in the living area looks out onto a shared courtyard. There’s a huge oak tree right outside, which is especially nice in autumn when the leaves change color. I also get quite a lot of natural light, so I’m pretty happy with the view. It’s not exactly a city skyline, but I prefer having some greenery outside.
If you could improve one thing about your home, what would it be?

Oh, definitely the bathroom. It’s quite small and a little dated, so I’d love to give it a complete makeover. If I could change anything, I’d probably replace the shower with a proper bathtub. I love the idea of having a long bath at the end of a busy day.
Do you plan to live there in the future?

Probably not forever. I really like the flat, and it’s perfect for me at the moment, but eventually I’d like somewhere with a little more outdoor space. Ideally, I’d love a small balcony or even a tiny garden, mainly because my cat would love having somewhere safe to sit outside. But for now, I’m quite happy where I am.

episodes.title: Teachers
transcript: Loading video…
Speaker: Finn
Do you have a favorite teacher?

Yeah, probably my high school history teacher, Mr. Carter. He had this habit of starting every lesson with some random story from history before actually getting into the textbook, so you never quite knew what you were going to get. I wasn’t particularly interested in history before his class, but he somehow made it really entertaining.
Do you remember your primary school teachers?

Yeah, I remember quite a few of them, actually. My primary school math teacher, Mrs. Wilson, stands out because she used to give us these little puzzles at the end of class if we finished our work early. I was really into those, so I still remember her pretty clearly.
Did you ever have a teacher you didn’t like? Why?

Yeah, there was one English teacher I didn’t particularly like. He was very serious and would sometimes interrupt you halfway through an answer if you made a mistake, which made me nervous about speaking in class. I’m sure he meant well, but I never really felt comfortable around him.
Have you ever had a teacher who influenced you a lot?

Not really, no. I mean, I had some good teachers, but I can’t say any of them had a huge influence on me outside of school. I mostly just remember the ones who made their classes enjoyable, rather than anyone who really changed the way I think or what I wanted to do.
What kind of teacher do you prefer?

I like teachers who are fairly relaxed but still know how to keep a class under control. I don’t mind a teacher being strict when they need to be, but I wouldn’t want someone who’s constantly checking whether you’re doing everything exactly right. I tend to learn better when I have a bit of freedom.
What qualities do you think a good teacher should have?

I’d say patience is probably the biggest one. Some students will understand something straight away, while others might need to hear the same explanation three or four times. I also think a good teacher needs a sense of humor. If a teacher can make you laugh occasionally, it makes a long class feel a lot shorter.
Do you think being a teacher is a difficult job?

Yeah, I think it’s much harder than it looks from the outside. When I was at school, I used to think teachers just showed up, taught for an hour, and went home. Now that I’m older, I realize there’s probably a huge amount of planning and marking that students never see. And having to deal with thirty teenagers at once can’t exactly be easy.
Do you want to be a teacher in the future?

Not really, no. I actually enjoy explaining things to people, but I don’t think I’d enjoy doing it with a whole classroom every day. I’d probably get more satisfaction from working on my own projects and having a bit more control over my schedule. So teaching isn’t really on my list of career options.
Speaker: Blondie
Do you have a favorite teacher?

Yeah, definitely. My high school English teacher, Ms. Davies, instantly comes to mind. She was just really down-to-earth and easy to talk to. Instead of just talking at us for an hour, she’d turn every lesson into a proper discussion where we could actually speak our minds. She just made you feel like what you had to say actually mattered, you know?
Do you remember your primary school teachers?

Vaguely, yeah. It’s mostly random memories, to be honest. I do remember my Year 3 teacher, Mr. Harrison, though, mostly because he’d bring his guitar into class every Friday afternoon and play music with us. I couldn’t tell you a single lesson we did back then, but I definitely remember how fun he made the classroom feel.
Did you ever have a teacher you didn’t like? Why?

Yeah, I had this math teacher in middle school who was really harsh. If you got a question wrong, he’d call you out in front of the whole class, which was just awful when you were twelve or thirteen. Everyone was basically walking on eggshells the entire period, so nobody ever wanted to raise their hand. It just totally ruined math for me.
Have you ever had a teacher who influenced you a lot?

Yeah, my high school art teacher had a huge impact on me. I used to be such a perfectionist and would stress out completely if a drawing didn’t turn out right. She really helped me chill out and showed me that making mistakes is just part of the process. That mindset actually stuck with me way beyond school, to be honest.
What kind of teacher do you prefer?

I’ve always done way better with teachers who are chill and easy to talk to, rather than super strict ones. If a teacher is approachable, you don’t feel like an idiot when you need to ask a question or if you don’t get something the first time around. Plus, when they’re actually into what they’re teaching, it just makes the whole class so much more engaging.
What qualities do you think a good teacher should have?

Patience is huge, for sure. Everyone learns at totally different speeds, so you can’t just have a one-size-fits-all approach. Being able to break down hard concepts into plain English is another big one. But honestly, I think just genuinely caring about the students as people makes the biggest difference.
Do you think being a teacher is a difficult job?

100%. Honestly, I think it’s one of the hardest jobs out there. It’s not just teaching the material—you’re basically managing thirty different personalities, dealing with piles of paperwork, and probably taking a lot of that stress home with you at the end of the day. It’s a lot to handle, and they definitely don’t get enough credit for it.
Do you want to be a teacher in the future?

Oh, definitely not! I mean, I have so much respect for what they do, but I just don’t have the patience for it. Standing in front of thirty kids all day and trying to keep their attention sounds absolutely exhausting. I’m definitely more of a behind-the-scenes person.

Speaker: Finn
Are you good at giving gifts?

To be honest, not really. I’m actually pretty bad at choosing gifts for people. I tend to overthink it and worry that they won’t like what I’ve bought. I usually end up asking someone else for advice, especially when I’m buying a gift for a close friend or a family member.
When do you usually give gifts to others?

Mostly on birthdays and other special occasions, like Christmas, Mother’s Day, or Father’s Day. I’m not really the type of person who gives gifts for no particular reason. I suppose I just tend to stick to the usual occasions because otherwise I probably wouldn’t know when to give someone something.
What kind of gifts do you usually give to people?

Usually something fairly practical. I might buy a friend some clothes, a book, or maybe something related to one of their hobbies. I’m not particularly creative when it comes to gifts, so I normally play it safe rather than trying to surprise someone with something unusual.
What do you consider when choosing a gift?

I mainly think about what the person actually likes and whether they’re likely to use it. I also consider how well I know them. If it’s a close friend, I’ll spend quite a bit of time thinking about it, but if it’s someone I don’t know that well, I’ll probably just go for something simple and safe.
Have you ever given someone a handmade gift?

No, I haven’t, actually. I’m not very good at making things, and I’ve never really had the patience for it either. I think a handmade gift can be really thoughtful, but if I tried to make something myself, there’s a good chance it wouldn’t look very good!
Do you prefer giving or receiving gifts?

I’d probably say receiving gifts. I know that sounds a bit selfish, but I find giving gifts quite stressful because I’m never completely sure whether I’ve chosen the right thing. Receiving one is much easier—you just have to smile and say thank you! Having said that, it is nice when you give someone something and they genuinely love it.
What is the best gift you have ever received?

Probably a pair of headphones that my parents gave me a few years ago. I’d mentioned that I needed a new pair, but I wasn’t expecting them to buy me any. I use them pretty much every day, so it was a really useful gift, and I was genuinely happy when I got them.
Do you think it is difficult to choose a suitable gift for someone?

Yeah, especially if you want to give them something meaningful. I think it’s actually quite difficult to know what someone really wants unless they’ve specifically told you. That’s probably why I’m not very good at giving gifts—I spend ages looking at different options and still end up wondering whether I’ve made the right choice.
Do expensive gifts better express your feelings?

Not really. I think the amount of thought you put into a gift matters more than how much it costs. Obviously, an expensive gift can be impressive, but if it’s something the person doesn’t actually want, then I don’t think it means very much. Sometimes a simple gift that shows you know the person well can mean much more.
Speaker: Blondie
Are you good at giving gifts?

I’d like to think so. I usually pay close attention to what my friends and family casually mention throughout the year, so when a special occasion rolls around, I can pick out something genuinely meaningful rather than just grabbing a last-minute gift card.
When do you usually give gifts to others?

The standard occasions, mainly—birthdays, Christmas, and the occasional housewarming or anniversary. That said, I’m also a big fan of “just because” gifts. If I’m out shopping and spot something that instantly reminds me of a close friend, I’ll get it for them right then and there.
What kind of gifts do you usually give to people?

It really depends on the recipient, but I tend to lean towards practical or experiential gifts. For instance, I might treat a coffee-loving friend to a subscription for specialty beans, or buy tickets to a gig for someone who loves live music. I prefer giving things people will actually use or remember.
What do you consider when choosing a gift?

My main focus is always on their personal tastes and lifestyle. I try to consider what they enjoy doing in their free time, or if there’s anything they’ve been needing lately. I also think about the emotional value—I want the item to show that I actually listen to them and understand what makes them tick.
Have you ever given someone a handmade gift?

Yes, quite a few times. Back when I was at university, I used to do a lot of digital illustration, so I made custom prints for my close friends and had them framed for their birthdays. It takes a bit of extra time and effort, but the personal touch always makes it far more memorable.
Do you prefer giving or receiving gifts?

Definitely giving. There’s something genuinely rewarding about watching someone open a present you’ve put real thought into and seeing their face light up. Receiving gifts is lovely, of course, but it can sometimes feel a bit awkward if you aren’t sure how to react in the moment.
What is the best gift you have ever received?

On my twentieth birthday, my older sister put together a photo album filled with pictures, ticket stubs, and handwritten notes from our childhood through to our recent trips together. It wasn’t the money that made it special, but the sheer amount of nostalgia and effort she put into it.
Do you think it is difficult to choose a suitable gift for someone?

It can be a real headache, especially if you don’t know the person particularly well or if they’re the type who already buys everything they need for themselves. In those cases, finding something unique without just giving them something generic can take a lot of guesswork.
Do expensive gifts better express your feelings?

Not necessarily. Just because a gift is expensive doesn’t mean it’s more thoughtful. A costly gift can sometimes feel a bit flashy, whereas a simple, inexpensive gift with some personal meaning can actually mean much more.

episodes.title: Watches
transcript: Speaker: Finn
Do you usually wear a watch?

No, not really. I don’t wear a watch at the moment because I usually check the time on my phone. Since I almost always have my phone with me, I don’t really feel the need to wear an additional device just to tell the time.
What kind of watch do you prefer to wear?

Even though I don’t currently wear a watch, I think I’d probably prefer a simple, traditional one. I like the classic look of analogue watches, and I think they can be a nice accessory without being too flashy.
When did you get your first watch?

To be honest, I don’t remember exactly when I got my first watch, but I think I was quite young, probably around seven or eight. It was just a basic watch, and I mainly wore it to school so I could learn how to tell the time.
Do you think watches are still popular nowadays?

Yes, definitely. Although people can easily check the time on their phones, watches are still popular, especially as fashion accessories. Smartwatches are also becoming increasingly common because they offer much more than simply telling the time.
Do you prefer traditional watches or smartwatches?

Personally, I prefer traditional watches. Even though smartwatches are obviously more practical, I think traditional watches look more stylish and timeless. They can also complement someone’s outfit quite nicely.
Why do some people like wearing expensive watches?

I think expensive watches can represent different things to different people. Some people see them as a symbol of success, while others genuinely appreciate the craftsmanship and design. In some cases, luxury watches can even hold their value, so people may see them as a worthwhile investment.
Have you ever received a watch as a gift?
No, I haven’t, actually. I’ve received other accessories as gifts, but never a watch. I wouldn’t mind getting one, though, especially if it was something simple and matched my personal style.
How often do you check the time during the day?

Quite often, to be honest. I usually check the time on my phone throughout the day, especially when I have somewhere to be or need to keep track of a schedule. I’d say it’s something I do almost automatically.
Do you think people will still wear watches in the future?

Yes, I think so. Technology may change the way watches are used, but I don’t think they’ll disappear. Smartwatches will probably become more advanced, while traditional watches will likely remain popular as fashion accessories and luxury items.
Speaker : Blondie
Do you usually wear a watch?

Yes, almost every single day. I have an Apple Watch that I wear constantly, mostly to keep track of my daily activity, check notifications quickly, and stay on top of my schedule while I’m on the move.
What kind of watch do you prefer to wear?

I definitely prefer smartwatches—specifically my Apple Watch. I love how functional and customizable it is. You can swap out the bands to match your outfit, and having all my health data and reminders right on my wrist is super convenient.
When did you get your first watch?

To be completely honest, I don’t really remember getting my first watch, or even if I actually had one growing up. Standard watches weren’t really something I paid attention to as a kid, so my Apple Watch is pretty much the first watch I’ve worn regularly.
Do you think watches are still popular nowadays?

Oh, absolutely. If anything, smartwatches have completely revitalized the market. A lot of people my age wear them daily for fitness tracking and productivity, while traditional watches remain popular as fashion accessories or luxury items.
Do you prefer traditional watches or smartwatches?

I definitely lean toward smartwatches. Being able to track my workouts, monitor my sleep, and see incoming calls or messages without pulling out my phone makes a smartwatch way more practical for my everyday lifestyle than a traditional analog watch.
Why do some people like wearing expensive watches?

I think for many people, luxury traditional watches are a major status symbol—they signal wealth, success, or refined taste. Beyond that, there’s a real appreciation for fine mechanical engineering and heritage, so people treat them like wearable art or valuable investments.
Have you ever received a watch as a gift?
Not that I can recall, no. I actually bought my Apple Watch for myself as a personal upgrade to stay organized and track my fitness.
How often do you check the time during the day?
Constantly! Since my Apple Watch is right on my wrist, I glance at it dozens of times a day—not just to check the time, but also to check timer alerts, calendar notifications, or my step count.
Do you think people will still wear watches in the future?

Without a doubt. Wristwear has evolved from simple timekeeping to advanced health monitoring and personal style. As wearable tech gets even smarter, people will definitely keep wearing them, whether for the technology or as classic fashion statements.

episodes.title: Patience and Politeness
transcript: Speaker: Finn
What do you think patience is?

I think patience is the ability to stay calm when things don’t go the way you want them to. For example, when you have to wait for something or deal with a difficult person without getting too frustrated.
Do you think patience is important?
Yes, definitely. I think it helps you deal with stressful situations and make better decisions. Without patience, it’s easy to react emotionally and say or do something you regret.
Do you think you are a patient person?
I’d say I’m fairly patient, especially with people. However, I can get a bit impatient when I’m waiting for a long time or when something is wasting my time for no good reason.
Have you ever lost your patience?
Yes, of course. I remember getting really frustrated when I was working on a group project and one person didn’t do their part. Eventually, I got annoyed and confronted them about it.
What kinds of situations make you lose your patience?
Probably when people waste my time or keep making the same mistake. I also get impatient when I’m stuck in a long queue, especially if I’m in a hurry.
Are you a polite person?
I’d like to think so. I always try to treat people with respect and use basic manners, like saying “please” and “thank you.” I think it’s just a natural habit for me.
Who taught you to be polite?
Mostly my parents, I think. They taught me basic manners when I was young, and I also learned a lot by watching how they treated other people.
Is it important to be polite?
Yes, I think so. Being polite makes it easier to get along with people and shows that you respect them. It can also make a bad situation a lot less stressful.
What do you do if others are not polite to you?

Honestly, it depends. If it’s a stranger, I usually just let it go because I don’t want to turn a small situation into an argument. But if someone I know is being rude to me, I’d probably ask them what their problem is.
Speaker: Blondie
What do you think patience is?

To me, patience is basically the ability to stay calm and composed when things aren’t going your way or when you’re forced to wait. It’s about not letting frustration get the better of you, whether you’re stuck in traffic or dealing with a difficult situation.
Do you think patience is important?

Absolutely. I think it’s especially important nowadays because everything moves so quickly, and it’s easy to lose your cool. Being patient helps you think things through instead of reacting impulsively, and it can definitely save you a lot of unnecessary stress.
Do you think you are a patient person?

For the most part, yeah, I’d say I am. I don’t really mind waiting in lines or taking the time to explain things to people. That said, if I’m running really late or dealing with a terrible internet connection, my patience can definitely wear a bit thin!
Have you ever lost your patience?

Oh, definitely—plenty of times! Just last week, I was trying to send an important file to a client before a deadline, and my laptop completely froze. I ended up getting so frustrated that I was practically yelling at my screen because I was already stressed about getting everything done on time.
What kinds of situations make you lose your patience?

I’d say situations where things are unnecessarily slow or disorganised really get to me. For example, standing in a ridiculously slow queue when only one checkout counter is open can be really frustrating. I also get annoyed when people are repeatedly late without giving me a heads-up.
Are you a polite person?
I like to think so! I always try to say “please” and “thank you,” hold doors for people, and generally treat others with respect. It’s just become second nature to me at this point.
Who taught you to be polite?

Mostly my parents. Ever since I was little, they were really big on manners. They led by example and taught me how to speak respectfully to older people and treat strangers kindly, so I think I picked up most of it from them.
Is it important to be polite?
Definitely. I think good manners just make everyday interactions much smoother. Being polite shows that you respect the person you’re talking to, and it usually creates a more positive atmosphere.
What do you do if others are not polite to you?

I usually try not to take it personally and just kill them with kindness. You never really know if someone’s having a bad day. But if they’re being genuinely rude or crossing a line, I’d probably say something and let them know I don’t appreciate the way they’re talking to me.

episodes.title: Parks and Gardens
transcript: Speaker: Finn
Do you often go to parks?

Not really, at the moment. I’m a university student, and there isn’t really a park near my university, so I don’t have much of a reason to go to one during the week. When I’m back home, though, there’s a park quite close to where I live, and I sometimes go there for a walk or to meet up with friends.
Is there a park or garden near your home?

Yeah, there’s a pretty nice park about a ten-minute walk from my house. It’s not huge, but it has quite a lot of trees, a walking path, and a small playground. I used to go there more often when I was younger, and I still go there occasionally when I’m back home.
What do you usually do when you visit a park?
